name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship covers the questions of who, or what, can be credited as an author when artificial intelligence systems help produce text, images, code, music, or research outputs. It examines the boundary between tool use and creative or intellectual contribution, including disclosure, originality, plagiarism, and accountability. The topic sits in governance, ethics, and research integrity because it affects journals, universities, funders, and publishers as much as it affects individual writers. It also asks how authorship norms should treat outputs that are generated, co-written, edited, or translated by models.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: AI and authorship covers the questions of who, or what, can be credited as an author when artificial intelligence systems help produce text, images, code, music, or research outputs. It examines the boundary between tool use and creative or intellectual contribution, including disclosure, originality, plagiarism, and accountability. The topic sits in governance, ethics, and research integrity because it affects journals, universities, funders, and publishers as much as it affects individual writers. It also asks how authorship norms should treat outputs that are generated, co-written, edited, or translated by models.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on generative models and the data, prompts, and fine-tuning that shape their outputs, together with the systems that record human and machine contributions. These include version control, document histories, editorial and peer review platforms, licensing records, and provenance metadata. Institutional policies, contributor statements, and disclosure forms are part of the infrastructure because they turn technical events into auditable claims. Training corpora, model documentation, and logs of model use also matter when authorship or originality is disputed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Researchers and integrity officers study AI and authorship through policy analysis, interviews, surveys, bibliometric studies, and audits of published outputs. They compare disclosure statements, contributor taxonomies such as CRediT, and journal or funder rules against actual practice. Technical methods include provenance tracking, watermarking, stylometry, and checks for text or image manipulation, though none is conclusive on its own. Case reviews and reproducibility checks help show where responsibility was assigned and where it was missing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on copyright, moral rights, patent inventorship, confidentiality, and liability, which vary by jurisdiction and by venue. Provenance is central because a claim of authorship depends on knowing what data, model, and human effort produced the work. Risks include undisclosed AI use, fabricated references, biased or harmful outputs, privacy breaches, and the dilution of accountability when no person can defend the result. Publishers, funders, and institutions increasingly require disclosure, but the rules remain uneven and often rely on self-reporting.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward clearer disclosure norms, better provenance infrastructure, and authorship criteria that separate assistance from responsibility. Journals, conferences, and funders are likely to keep revising their policies as generative tools become embedded in writing and review. Technical measures such as watermarking and signed provenance records may support provenance, but they will not settle authorship on their own. International coordination and training for researchers are likely to grow, alongside continued debate about whether non-human systems can ever hold rights or duties.
